and Joiners of America (Local 2002), filed a petition seeking to amend Certification 84.
Local 2002 seeks to designate itself as the exclusive bargaining agent for a unit of
employees assigned to the Road, Land Fill, and Maintenance Departments employed by
Putnam County.
On June 4, the Commission -appointed hearing officer issued an order
recommending that the petition be granted and Certification 84 be amended to designate
Local 2002 as the certified bargaining agent. The hearing officer noted that the instant
case was similar to recent petitions approved by the Commission. See, e.g., In re
Petition of Local Union No. 2038 of the United Brotherhood of Carpenters and Joiners of
America, to Amend Certification No. 103, 41 FPER If 328 (2015); In re Petition of Local
Union No. 2502 of the United Brotherhood of Carpenters and Joiners of America, to
Amend Certification No. 309, 41 FPER 11329 (2015). No parties filed exceptions to the
hearing officer's recommendation.

AC-2015-001
Upon consideration, we accept the hearing officer's findings of fact and his
analysis of the dispositive legal issues and conclusions of law. § 120.57(1)(1), Fla. Stat.
(2014). Accordingly, the hearing officer's recommended order is incorporated as part of
this final order and the petition is GRANTED. Certification 84 is amended to reflect the
name of the certified bargaining agent as Local Union No. 2002 of the United
Brotherhood of Carpenters and Joiners of America.
This order may be appealed to the appropriate district court of appeal. A notice of
appeal must be received by the Commission and the district court of appeal within thirty
days from the date of this order. Except in cases of indigency, the court will require a
filing fee and the Commission will require payment for preparing the record on appeal.
Further explanation of the right to appeal is provided in Sections 120.68 and 447.504,
Florida Statutes (2014), and the Florida Rules of Appellate Procedure.

AND JOINERS OF AMERICA, TO RECOMMENDED ORDER

AMEND CERTIFICATION NO. 84.
Jason H. Weitzel, Oshkosh, Wisconsin, representative for Local Union No. 2002 of the
United Brotherhood of Carpenters and Joiners of America.
Rick Leary, Palatka, representative for Putnam County Board of County Commissioners.
RIX, Hearing Officer.
On May 11, 2015, Local Union No. 2002 of the United Brotherhood of Carpenters
and Joiners of America (Local 2002), filed a petition to amend Certification 84 to
designate it as bargaining agent for a bargaining unit of employees assigned to the
Road, Land Fill, and Maintenance Departments of Putnam County (County).' On
May 18, the Commission appointed the undersigned as the hearing officer in this case.
On May 21, I directed the County to file a response to the petition by the close of
business on June 1. I notified the County that if it did not file a response I would assume
that it does not object to the requested amendment to Certification 84. To date, no
response has been filed.
'Local 2002 is currently registered with the Commission. See In re Aplication for
Registration of Local Union No. 2002 of the United Brotherhood of Carpenters and
Joiners of America, Case No. OR -15 -003 (Fla. PERC Apr. 2015).

AC-2015-001
In its petition, Local 2002 seeks to amend Certification 84 to reflect its recent
affiliation with "Carpenters Industrial Council" and be designated as "Local Union
No. 2002 of the United Brotherhood of Carpenters and Joiners of America." The
Commission's threshold test for analyzing a petition seeking to amend a certification to
reflect a change in the employee organization is as follows:
When an amendment to a certification petition has been filed, the
Commission will first consider whether the amendment is a mere
name change. If it is, the amendment is allowed so long as it is
consistent with the organization's constitution and by -laws. If the
change is more than a change in name, the Commission must
decide whether a question concerning representation is raised. If
so, a representation election is necessary before the amendment
can be made. Finally, if the proposed amendment is more than a
name change, but does not constitute a question concerning
representation, then the amendment will be allowed so long as the
procedure used to bring about the change reflects the desires of
affected employees. See In re Southern States Police Benevolent
Association, Inc., to Amend Certification 1079, 23 FPER 1128029
(1996).
See In re International Union of Painters and Allied Trades, AFL -CIO, Local Union 2301
to Amend Certification 986, 27 FPER 1132129 at 293 (2001).
The Commission's records reveal that Public Employees, #2002 was originally
certified by the Commission in 1975 as the exclusive bargaining agent for the employees
assigned to the County's Road, Land Fill, and Maintenance Departments. See Public
Employees, #2002, and Putnam County, Case No. 8H -RA- 752 -0085 (Fla. PERC July 2,
1975) (Certification 84). In 1986, the Commission amended Certification 84 to designate
the "Florida Council of Industrial and Public Employees, Local 2002, United Brotherhood
of Carpenters and Joiners of America, AFL -CIO" as the certified bargaining agent of
2

AC-2015-001
these employees. See In re Florida Council of Industrial and Public Employees,
13 FPER ¶ 18029 at 107 (1986). That case involved a change in affiliation of district
councils from the "Southern Council of Industrial Workers" to the "Florida Council of
Industrial and Public Employees."
In the instant petition, Local 2002 seeks to amend Certification 84 to reflect its
recent affiliation with "Carpenters Industrial Council" and revise its name and be
designated as "Local Union No. 2002 of the United Brotherhood of Carpenters and
Joiners of America." The petition and supporting documents state that on August 15 and
October 8, 2014, United Brotherhood of Carpenters and Joiners of America General
President Douglas J. McCarron ordered that Local 2002 become affiliated with the
"Carpenters Industrial Council" pursuant to his authority under Section 6A of the UBC
constitution. McCarron's directive was permitted by Section 6A of the UBC Constitution,
subject to an appeal process to the General Executive Board (Board). McCarron's
directive was not appealed to the Board. The petition also avers that the vested rights of
the bargaining unit members have not been affected. The members' right to attend and
participate in meetings, vote, nominate candidates, be nominated, and run for office has
not been changed. In effect, Local 2002 is no longer affiliated with the "Florida Council
of Industrial and Public Employees" and it desires to change its name to conform to its
registered name and to reflect its change in intermediate council affiliation.
The petition is similar to several recent petitions approved by the Commission.
See, e.q., In re Petition of Local Union No. 2038 of the United Brotherhood of Carpenters
and Joiners of America, to Amend Certification No. 103, 41 FPER ¶ 328 (2015) (granting
3

AC-2015-001
union's amendment of certification petition seeking to reflect a change in intermediate
council affiliation for union representing full -time county road and bridge department
employees); In re Petition of Local Union No. 2502 of the United Brotherhood of
Carpenters and Joiners of America, to Amend Certification No. 309, 41 FPER ¶ 309
(2015) (granting union's amendment of certification petition seeking to reflect a change in
council affiliation and to conform its certification to its registered name). Based upon the
evidence presented, I recommend that the Commission grant the petition and amend
Certification 84 to designate "Local Union No. 2002 of the United Brotherhood of
Carpenters and Joiners of America" as the certified bargaining agent for the affected
County employees.
Any party may file exceptions to my recommended order, but exceptions must be
received by the Commission within fifteen days from the date of this order. See Fla.
Admin. Code Rule 28- 106.217(1). An extension of time for filing exceptions will not be
granted unless good cause is shown.

accordance with Florida Administrative Code Rule 28- 106.216 and SERVED on all
y
parties this day of June, 2015.

FRATERNAL ORDER OF POLICE, HEARING OFFICER'S
:
TO AMEND CERTIFICATION NO. 345. RECOMMENDED ORDER
:
Kathleen M. Phillips, Miami, attorney for William Nichols Lodge #8 (Miami Beach),
Fraternal Order of Police.
Raul J. Aguila, Miami Beach, attorney for City of Miami Beach.
RIX, Hearing Officer.
On August 3, 2015, the William Nichols Lodge #8 (Miami Beach), Fraternal Order
of Police (Lodge #8), filed an amendment to certification petition pursuant to Section
447.207(6), Florida Statutes (2015).1 The petition seeks to amend certification 345 to
reflect Florida State Lodge, Fraternal Order of Police, Inc.'s (Florida State Lodge)
designation of Lodge #8 as the certified bargaining representative of a bargaining unit of
City of Miami Beach (City) rank -and -file law enforcement personnel. See Florida State
Lodge, Fraternal Order of Police v. City of Miami Beach, Case No. 8H -RC- 766 -2085 (Fla.
PERC Aug. 12, 1977) (designating Florida State Lodge as the certified bargaining
representative of the City's rank- and -file law enforcement personnel). On August 6, the
Commission appointed the undersigned as hearing officer in this case.
'The Petitioner's name has been amended to conform to the name in which it is
currently registered. See In Re William Nichols Lodge #8 (Miami Beach), Fraternal Order
of Police, (Fla. PERC, July 31, 2015).

AC-2015-002
On August 14, I directed the City to file a response to the petition by the close of
business on August 24 and serve a copy on Lodge #8. I notified the City that if it did not
file a response, I would assume that the petition does not raise disputed issues of
material fact and that the City does not oppose the granting of the petition. To date, no
response has been filed.
The Commission has approved amendments of certification to substitute a local
union for its parent organization when two criteria are met: (1) the union demonstrates
that there will be substantial continuity in the representation of the members of the
bargaining unit and (2) the substitution has been approved by the members of the
bargaining unit. See In re Gator Lodge 67, Inc., Fraternal Order of Police to Amend
Certification No. 1053, 31 FPER 132 (2005); In re Fraternal Order of Police, Clearwater
Lodge #10, Inc., to Amend Certification No. 239, 29 FPER 92 (2003). Such approval is
evidenced by a showing that all members of the bargaining unit were provided with:
(a) reasonable notice of the proposed change, (b) a reasonable opportunity for
discussion of the change prior to a vote, and (c) a voting procedure which fairly reflects
the employees' desires. See In re Rockledge Professional Firefighters Association,
15 FPER ¶ 20195 (1989).
As noted above, the Florida State Lodge was originally certified by the
Commission in 1977 as the exclusive bargaining agent of the regular full -time and regular
part-time sworn lieutenants and lower- ranking police personnel. According to the petition
2

AC-2015-002
and supporting documentation, Lodge #8 is a subordinate lodge of the Florida State
Lodge, and is a labor organization. The Florida State Lodge has designated Lodge #8 to
negotiate and administer a succession of collective bargaining agreements and to be
otherwise responsible for representing the bargaining unit with respect to rates of pay,
benefits, and terms and conditions of employment.
For over thirty years Lodge #8 has been the de facto bargaining representative for
the bargaining unit through its officers, committees, and designees. Lodge #8 has
maintained control of the bargaining unit's finances. It collects, maintains, and expends
all bargaining unit monies, including membership dues. It has negotiated and executed
collective bargaining agreements and administered those agreements, including the
current agreement, with the City. Lodge #8 has provided representation to bargaining
unit employees for processing all grievances, representing them in internal affairs,
investigations, and disciplinary matters. The City has been negotiating with Lodge #8 in
regards to the unit for over thirty years and has recognized Lodge #8 as the certified
bargaining agent.
Lodge #8 is governed by the same constitution and by -laws of its parent
organization, the Florida State Lodge. The proposed amendment to substitute the
certification from the Florida State Lodge to its subordinate Lodge #8 will not change the
manner in which business has been conducted regarding rates of pay, benefits, and all
terms and conditions of employment for bargaining unit employees and there will be
substantial continuity in the representation of the bargaining unit employees because
3

AC-2015-002
Lodge #8 will continue to negotiate and administer the collective bargaining agreements
and represent bargaining unit employees in grievances and disciplinary matters. The
same officers will be conducting business on behalf of the bargaining unit.
The proposed amendment will formalize the de facto bargaining representative
status of Lodge #8. None of the bargaining unit members will have any diminution in
rights as a result of substituting the parent organization, Florida State Lodge, with
Lodge #8 and it will continue representing bargaining unit members in the identical
fashion.
The national and state lodges' constitutions provide for the chartering of
subordinate lodges such as Lodge #8. The establishment and transfer of responsibilities
from the national and state lodges to subordinate lodges is contemplated by and
accomplished in accordance with constitutional provisions adopted by the membership,
including the membership of Lodge #8. The governing documents do not require notice
and a vote to approve the substitution, as this is a change involving internal union
matters with no impact upon the representational or membership interests or rights of
bargaining unit employees. The amendment to certification is a formalization of rights
and responsibilities already performed by Lodge #8.
Based upon the undisputed facts, I conclude that Lodge #8 has met the first prong
of the test by demonstrating that there will be substantial continuity in the representation
of the members of the bargaining unit. The undisputed evidence shows that Lodge #8
has been the de facto bargaining agent for the affected employees through its
4

AC-2015-002
negotiation of collective bargaining agreements, representation of bargaining unit
employees in grievance and disciplinary matters, and in executing the collective
bargaining agreements for the affected employees. It will continue these functions
should the petition be granted. The practical effect of the proposed amendment is to
formalize the de facto bargaining representative status of Lodge #8.
As to the second prong of the test I note that there is no evidence presented
showing approval by the bargaining unit members through notice of the proposed
change, a reasonable opportunity for discussion of the change, and a voting procedure
which fairly reflects the employees' desires. However, the national and state lodge
constitutions authorize the chartering of subordinate lodges, and the establishment and
transfer of responsibilities from the national and state lodges is contemplated by and
accomplished in accordance with constitutional provisions adopted by the membership.
These provisions do not require notice and a vote to approve substitutions under the
circumstances herein.
Therefore, the absence of notice and a vote should not be fatal to the petition
under the circumstances herein. See, e.q., In re Gator Lodge 67, Inc., Fraternal Order of
Police to Amend Certification No. 1053, 31 FPER at 299 (2005); In re Fraternal Order of
Police, Clearwater Lodge #10, Inc., 29 FPER at 236. Based on the foregoing, I
recommend that the Commission grant the instant petition and amend certification 345
reflect the substitution of Lodge #8 for the Florida State Lodge as the certified bargaining
representative.
5

AC-2015-002
Any party may file exceptions to my recommended order, but exceptions must be
received by the Commission within fifteen days from the date of this order. See Fla.
Admin. Code Rule 28- 106.217(1). An extension of time for filing exceptions will not be
granted unless good cause is shown.

accordance with Florida Administrative Code Rule 28- 106.216 and SERVED on all

Corrections (Agency) to reinstate Lawrence Young and provide him with back pay and
benefits, less any compensation and earnings he would not have received had his
employment with the Agency not been interrupted. See Young v. Department of

back pay on PERC Form 18.

conducted between Tallahassee and West Palm Beach. All parties were afforded the
opportunity to call witnesses, cross -examine witnesses, and fully participate.' Young
entered three exhibits into evidence and he testified on his own behalf. The Agency did

not offer any exhibits or witness testimony. The parties filed written post -hearing

hearing revolved around how much back pay Young was entitled to receive and whether
he should be reimbursed for the out of pocket costs he paid to obtain health insurance.

issued its Order Vacating Agency Action on June 30. Young returned to duty with the
Agency on July 17. The total back pay exposure period is February 17, 2015, through
and including July 16, 2015. (Stipulation)
2. Prior to his dismissal, Young was employed as a Correctional Probation
Officer in the West Palm Beach Circuit Office.
3. Young worked an eight hour workday /forty hour workweek schedule. His
gross wages were $18.99 hourly or $1,518.71 bi- weekly. (Stipulation)2
2There is a slight discrepancy between the bi- weekly amount calculated from the
hourly amount and the stipulated bi- weekly amount. ($18.99 per hour x 40 hours a week
x 2 weeks = $1.519.20 verses stipulated bi- weekly amount of $1,518.71). Because the
calculations include partial weeks and the need to consider daily amounts, I have used
2

(Relates to CS-2015-029)
4. The initial grace period lasted from February 17, through and including
March 18. (Stipulation)3
5. Young did not take a disbursement from the Florida Retirement System and
he is eligible for reinstatement in the Florida Retirement System. (Stipulation)
6. There were twenty -two work days during the initial grace period. Young is
entitled to $3,342.24 in gross back pay, less taxes and any other lawful deductions, for
the initial grace period.
7. Young is also entitled to back pay for the second grace period, which
started on June 30, when the Commission entered its Order Vacating Agency Action and
July 17, when he returned to work. June 30 was a Tuesday, so Young is also entitled to
receive back pay for Monday, June 29, pursuant to recent changes in Commission case
law.4
8. There were fourteen work days during the second grace period. Young is
entitled to $2,126.88 in gross back pay, less taxes and any other lawful deductions, for
the second grace period.
the stipulated hourly amount in making my calculations. Any difference between the two
is negligible.
Pursuant to well -established case law, an employee is not required to seek
alternative work for the first thirty days after his or her dismissal. Sabria v. Department of
Business and Professional Regulation, 15 FCSR 682 (2000). This is commonly referred
to as the initial grace period.
4In Vickery v. Department of Corrections, 30 FCSR 79 (2015), the Commission
held that an employee is entitled to back pay for the entire week in which the Commission
issues the order reinstating the employee to agency employment.

9. For the remaining portion of the back pay exposure period from March 19
through June 26, which covers seventy -three work days, Young is required to provide

evidence that an employee conducted a good faith job search.

compensation. Young credibly testified that to be eligible for unemployment benefits he
was required to perform at least five job searches every week. Every week, he was
required to enter information into the computer detailing where he looked for work, when
he looked for work, the type of position that was being applied for, and the status of the
hiring decision.
11. Young credibly testified that he conducted a good faith job search during
the remainder of the back pay exposure period because he was required to apply for at
least five jobs each week to be entitled to unemployment compensation.
12. Young started his job search immediately upon his dismissal, but he was
not immediately approved for unemployment compensation. Most of his applications
were done online or through the People's First System for state jobs. Despite these
applications, Young did not receive any interviews.
13. Young received a total of $3,850.00 in unemployment compensation during
the back pay period. This was the maximum amount that Young was entitled to receive
and the benefit was exhausted.
4

BP-2015-010
(Relates to CS-2015-029)
14. Young provided documentation from Florida Department of Economic
Opportunity showing that he was paid unemployment benefits in ten weeks. The weeks
listed in the documentation were the weeks starting April 13, April 20, April 27, May 4,
May 11, May 18, May 25, June 1, June 8, and June 15, 2015. Young was paid a total of
$2,750.00 for these ten weeks. The difference between the $3,850.00 total amount
Young was paid and the $2,750.00 for the ten weeks expressly listed on the
documentation is $1,100.00. This amount reflects four additional weeks that Young was
eligible to receive unemployment compensation.

documentation from the Department of Economic Opportunity, provide credible evidence
of a good faith effort to mitigate his job loss. Therefore, Young is entitled to payment for
the remaining portion of the back pay exposure period from March 19 through June 26,
which amounts to $11,090.16 in gross back pay, less taxes and any other lawful
deductions.
16. Young was provided health insurance coverage while he was employed by
the Agency. After he was terminated, his Agency -provided health care coverage lapsed
as of March 31.
17. Young was required by federal law to obtain health insurance coverage for
his family or face tax penalties.
18. Young purchased health insurance from Cigna. His premium was $504.97
per month.
5

BP-2015-010
(Relates to CS-2015-029)
19. Young purchased health insurance for four months, April, May, June, and
July 2015.
20. Young's total cost for health insurance during the back pay period was
$2,019.88.
21. Young was able to return to his state offered insurance through Blue
Cross /Blue Shield starting in August 2015. Young wrote a check for $216.11 in order to
"catch up on the total premiums." Young characterized this as the amount he had to pay
each month before being terminated. According to an email Young entered into
evidence, along with a copy of the check for $216.11, the amount consists of $180.00 for
his August health insurance and $26.11 for the first half of September 2015 dental
insurance.
ANALYSIS
In a back pay proceeding, the Commission is required to approximate the earnings
an employee would have received absent his improper discharge. See Florida State
Lodge, Fraternal Order of Police v. Town of Pembroke Park, 10 FPER If 15001 (1983),
recon. denied, 10 FPER 1115072 (1984), affd in pertinent part, 501 So. 2d 1294 (Fla.
4th DCA 1987).
The parties reached stipulations on many of the variables necessary to calculate
the amount of Young's back pay compensation, such as his rate of pay, work schedule,
and the starting and ending dates for his two grace periods. For the initial grace period,
6

BP-2015-010
(Relates to CS-2015-029)
Young is entitled to $3,342.24 in gross back pay, less taxes and any other lawful
deductions. For the second grace period, Young is entitled to $2,126.88 in gross back
pay, less taxes and any other lawful deductions.
Moreover, he provided documentation from the Department of Economic
Opportunity about the benefits he received that showed he was eligible to receive
unemployment. He was paid the maximum amount allowed, $3,850.00. Therefore, for
the remaining back pay exposure period Young is entitled to $11,090.16 in gross back
pay, less taxes and any other lawful deductions.
In its post- hearing document, the Agency argues that Young should not be entitled
to any back pay outside of the two grace periods because his testimony and
documentation were not precise as to exactly where he applied.5 The Agency recognizes
that the Commission's recent decision in Vickery v. Department of Corrections, 30 FCSR
79 (2015) allowed employees to introduce evidence of unemployment compensation as
evidence of a good faith job search. However, the Agency also suggests that the
Commission's standard on the use of such evidence was "stringent" because the
employee in that case provided testimony as to his job searches, names, dates, and
ways of communication, in addition to evidence of his unemployment. I disagree. The
entire objective behind the Commission's decision in Vickery was to relax an analysis that
had become far too stringent. The Commission specifically held that back pay
5The Agency incorrectly states that he could not remember how many interviews
he went on. Young testified that he did not receive any interviews.
7

BP-2015-010
(Relates to CS-2015-029)
proceedings are remedial in nature and reasonable doubts should be resolved in favor of
the employee because it was the employer's wrongful conduct that initially caused the
loss of employment. Here, in addition to the documentation that Young provided that
showed that he had satisfied the Department of Economic Opportunity's expectations on
seeking employment, Young also credibly testified that he applied to at least five
employers a week, mostly online or through People's First, and that he provided
information on where he applied, when he applied, and the status of his application via
computer to receive his benefit. Under these circumstances, I am satisfied that Young
attempted to mitigate his job loss under the requirements outlined in Vickery.
For the two grace periods and the remaining back pay period, the total amount of
gross back pay is $16,559.28, minus the $3,850 in unemployment compensation he
received. Consequently, Young should be paid a total of $12,709.28 in back pay, less
any taxes and other lawful deductions.
As for Young's out -of- pocket insurance costs, at hearing, the Agency suggested
that Young may not be entitled to any recovery of the amount he spent on health
insurance. However, the Commission has held that employees are entitled to
reimbursement for health insurance coverage as a cornponent of back pay. See Miron v.
Amalgamated Transit Union, Local 1593, 34 FPER IT 268 (2007) (citing Stanfield v.
Department of Health and Rehabilitative Services, 9 FCSR 11196 at 815 (1994)); see also
Smith v. Department of Corrections, 41 FPER 11202 (2014). Young paid a premium of
$504.97 for the four months he was out of work, for a total of $2,019.88. In its post-
8

BP-2015-010
(Relates to CS-2015-029)
hearing filing, the Agency suggests that this amount should be reduced by the amount of
$864.44 ($216.11 /month x 4 months) based on Young's testimony that this represented
the amount that normally would have been withheld from his paycheck for health
insurance had he remained employed. Young's testimony, however, conflicted with the
documentary evidence he provided, which indicated that of the $216.11, only $180 was
attributable to his health insurance premium and the remaining amount appeared to be
for half a month of dental insurance. Therefore, Young is entitled to $2,019.88, minus an
offset of $720 ($180 /month x 4 months), for a total of $1,299.88 to cover the cost of
health insurance above what he would normally have paid had he remained employed by
the Agency.
CONCLUSIONS OF LAW
1. Young is entitled to $12,709.28 in gross back pay, minus taxes and other
lawful deductions.
2. Young is entitled to $1,299.88 for health insurance costs that occurred
during the back pay period.
RECOMMENDATION
I recommend that the Commission adopt the foregoing recommended order and
award Young back pay and benefits as set forth above.

recommendation (if any) in this order without first reviewing an official transcript of the
hearing. Any party who desires the Commission to review the transcript must file one
along with the exceptions.

STATE OF FLORIDA
PUBLIC EMPLOYEES RELATIONS COMMISSION
CARL RICHARDSON,
Employee, Case No. BP- 2015 -012
(Relates to CS- 2015 -065)
v.
FINAL ORDER
DEPARTMENT OF CORRECTIONS,
Order Number: 15CS -174
Agency.
Date Issued: December 8, 2015
Matthew O. Ward, Tallahassee, attorney representing employee.
Sena M. Bailes, Tallahassee, attorney representing agency.
On October 19, 2015, the hearing officer issued his recommended order in this
back pay case. In that order, he concluded that Carl Richardson was entitled to back pay
in the amount of $15,894.07, less lawful deductions, plus interest at the lawful rate. The
Department of Corrections (Agency) sought two extensions of time to file exceptions to
the hearing officer's recommended order, which were granted. On November 12, the
Agency filed a single exception challenging a portion of the hearing officer's
recommended back pay calculation involving overtime pay. The Agency also filed a copy
of the transcript from the October 7 hearing. Richardson did not file any exceptions and
did not respond to the Agency's exceptions.
As part of the $15,894.07 back pay award, the hearing officer recommended that
Richardson be paid $2,385.60 in overtime pay. The hearing officer based this amount on
a factual finding that there was a significant need for employees to work overtime at the
institution where Richardson was employed.

Case No. BP- 2015 -012
(Relates to CS- 2015 -065)
In factual finding number nine, the hearing officer found, in relevant part, that
officers could usually work as much overtime as they desired at Apalachee Correctional
Institution (ACI), where Richardson was employed. Richardson's own overtime work
varied and depended on how tired he was and what was happening in his life at any
given time. Richardson usually attempted to work fifteen to twenty hours of overtime a
month, but in December 2014, he worked eighty hours. Furthermore, between April 24
and May 13, 2015, he worked 34.5 hours of overtime. Richardson was planning on
working more overtime in the summer to make extra money. Richardson was paid at the
overtime rate of one and one -half times the regular hourly rate. There is competent
substantial evidence to support the hearing officer's factual findings regarding the
frequency and availability of overtime at ACI, Richardson's history of overtime work, and
his plans to continue working more overtime over the summer. (T. 7, 27 -33, 57, 60 -62;
Employee's Exhibit 10)
Based on these factual findings and Richardson's history of working overtime, the
hearing officer made an additional inference in factual finding number nine that
Richardson would have worked an average of twenty -four hours of overtime per month
during the back pay period. In his analysis, the hearing officer established that the
evidence showed that Richardson worked overtime on a consistent basis prior to being
dismissed and that he would have had the same opportunity to work overtime during the
back pay period. The back pay period was approximately three and one -half months.
2

Case No. BP- 2015 -012
(Relates to CS- 2015 -065)
Therefore, the hearing officer concluded that Richardson was entitled to eighty -four hours
of overtime pay at the rate of $28.40, which amounted to $2,385.60.
In support of this conclusion, the hearing officer cited the Commission's decision in
Shiver v. Department of Corrections, 30 FCSR 85 (2015). While the Commission did not
expressly address the issue of overtime in our final order in Shiver, we did adopt the
hearing officer's factual findings, analysis, conclusions of law, and recommendation. In
analyzing the issue of overtime, the hearing officer noted that the employee provided
evidence regarding the history of her overtime pay. Shiver, 30 FCSR at 89. She also
noted that no evidence was presented to support a finding that the employee would not
have continued this level of overtime had she remained employed. Id. The hearing
officer, however, did not award the employee more overtime than she had been
previously paid based on her testimony that she would have worked more overtime than
she had previously. Id.
In its exception, the Agency challenges the hearing officer's findings and analysis
regarding Richardson's case and attempts to distinguish the Shiver case. The Agency
argues that there is no competent substantial evidence for the hearing officer's
conclusion that Richardson would have had the same opportunity to work overtime during
the back pay period. The Agency bases its argument, in part, on the testimony of ACI's
warden, who suggested that overtime is not necessarily guaranteed. The Agency
request that we reject the hearing officer's findings, conclusions, and recommendation
related to overtime, and that Richardson be given no back pay associated with overtime.
3

Case No. BP- 2015 -012
(Relates to CS- 2015 -065)
We disagree with the Agency's assertions. The Commission has long held that
overtime pay can form a component of an overall back pay award. In the Commission's
seminal case on back pay proceedings, the Commission expressly noted that back pay
"includes not only the wages [an employee] would have earned but also other sums of
money or the equivalent [the employee] would have received, such as bonuses, raises,
and overtime pay." See Florida State Lodge, Fraternal Order of Police v. Town of
Pembroke Park, 10 FPER 1115001 (1983), aff d in pertinent part, 501 So. 2d 1294 (Fla.
4th DCA 1987) (emphasis added). Therefore, where the evidence supports an award of
back pay associated with overtime, it is appropriate to include it in the gross back pay
award given to an employee.
The question, therefore, is whether the evidence in this case supports including an
award for overtime pay in the gross back pay award that Richardson is entitled to receive.
"lt is the hearing officer's function to consider all the evidence presented, resolve
conflicts, judge credibility of witnesses, draw permissible inferences from the evidence,
and reach ultimate findings of fact based on competent, substantial evidence." See
Heifetz v. Department of Business Regulation, 475 So. 2d 1277, 1281 (Fla. 1st DCA
1985). A finding of fact can only be rejected when there is no competent substantial
evidence from which the finding can be reasonably inferred. Boyd v. Department of
Revenue, 682 So. 2d 1117, 1118 (Fla. 4th DCA 1996).
Here, there is competent substantial evidence to support the hearing officer's
factual findings regarding the frequency and availability of overtime at ACI, Richardson's
4

Case No. BP- 2015 -012
(Relates to CS- 2015 -065)
history of overtime work, and his plans to continue working more overtime over the
summer. These findings also support the hearing officer's inference that Richardson
would have continued to have the opportunity to work overtime during the back pay
period. To the extent that the warden's testimony conflicted with these findings,' it was
the hearing officer's responsibility to resolve the conflict. We cannot reweigh conflicting
evidence and substitute alternate facts, even if we were inclined to do so. Heifetz,
475 So. 2d at 1281.
The Agency also argues that the hearing officer's reliance on Shiver is misplaced.
The Agency notes that the hearing officer in Shiver stated that there was no evidence
presented to support a finding that the employee's overtime would not have continued. In
the instant case, the Agency argues the warden testified that there was no way of
knowing whether Richardson would have continued to work the same level of overtime.
The Agency also cites to the fact that the hearing officer in Shiver did not award the
employee overtime above what she had historically earned.
We believe that the hearing officers' orders in Shiver and the instant case are in
accord with one another and the Agency's attempt to distinguish them is unavailing.
While there is no certainty that a discharged employee would work overtime, the hearing
officers' inferences in both Shiver and the instant case were both wedded to reasonable
inferences based on the employees' history of working overtime. The hearing officer in
1We would expressly note that the warden also testified that he could not recall
there being any times when ACI did not use overtime given the vacancies at the
institution. (T. 62)
5

Case No. BP- 2015 -012
(Relates to CS- 2015 -065)
Shiver did not award the employee an amount of overtime above what she had
historically earned. Similarly, in the instant case, there were periods where Richardson
worked more overtime than the average of twenty -four hours of overtime per month that
the hearing officer recommended. This was a reasonable average based on the
evidence presented. Based on the foregoing, the Agency's exception is denied.
We also take this opportunity to ratify the hearing officers' methodology in this
case and in Shiver. Where the amount of overtime an employee historically worked may
have fluctuated, it cannot be said with absolute accuracy how much overtime a
discharged employee would have worked. Nevertheless, it is appropriate to award
overtime pay in addition to the normal wages where the evidence demonstrates a history
of overtime pay. Based on the evidence presented, a hearing officer's conclusion based
on historical averages or a ratio of past overtime pay is an acceptable substitute for an
exact calculation. To grant a discharged employee nothing in the way of overtime pay
under such circumstances would reward the Agency for its wrongful conduct in
discharging the employee.
Upon review of the complete record, the Commission finds that the hearing
officer's findings of fact are supported by competent substantial evidence received in a
proceeding that satisfies the essential requirements of the law. § 120.57(1)(1), Fla. Stat.
(2015). Furthermore, we agree with the hearing officer's analysis of the dispositive legal
issues, his conclusions of law, and his recommendations. Therefore, the hearing officer's
recommended order is incorporated herein. § 120.57(1)(1), Fla. Stat. The Agency is
6

Case No. BP- 2015 -012
(Relates to CS- 2015 -065)
directed to pay Richardson back pay in the amount of $15,894.07, less lawful deductions,
plus interest at the lawful rate until paid.
This order and the Commission's August 25, 2015, Order Vacating Agency Action
may be appealed to the appropriate district court of appeal.2 A notice of appeal must be
received by the Commission and the district court of appeal within thirty days from the
date of this order. Except in cases of indigency, the court will require a filing fee and the
Commission will require payment for preparing the record on appeal. Further explanation
of the right to appeal is provided in Sections 120.68 and 447.504, Florida Statutes (2015),
and the Florida Rules of Appellate Procedure.
It is so ordered.
DELGADO and POOLE, Commissioners, concur.

STATE OF FLORIDA
PUBLIC EMPLOYEES RELATIONS COMMISSION
CARL RICHARDSON,
Employee, Case No. BP- 2015 -012
(Relates to CS- 2015 -065)
v.
HEARING OFFICER'S
DEPARTMENT OF CORRECTIONS, RECOMMENDED ORDER
:
Agency.
Matthew O. Ward, Tallahassee, attorney representing employee.
Sena M. Bailes, Tallahassee, attorney representing agency.
SHOWALTER, Hearing Officer.
On August 25, 2015, the Commission issued an order vacating Carl Richardson's
dismissal from employment with the Department of Corrections (Agency) and awarding
Richardson back pay. A back pay case was established and a hearing was scheduled.
On October 7, a telephone hearing was conducted between Tallahassee and
Chattahoochee. All parties were provided with an opportunity to appear, present
evidence, examine witnesses, and fully participate in the hearing. Richardson presented
an oral closing argument, which I have carefully considered in preparing this order. The
Agency did not file a post- hearing document. A transcript of the hearing was not filed.
FINDINGS OF FACT
1. At the time of his dismissal, Richardson was a correctional officer sergeant
working at Apalachee Correctional Institution (ACI). He worked the 7:00 p.m. to
'The parties' stipulations are included in my findings of fact.

BP-2015-012
(Relates to CS-2015-065)
7:00 a.m. shift. His work schedule consisted of three days on -duty and two days off -duty
followed by two days on -duty and three days off -duty. (Stipulation)
2. The back pay period runs from May 14, 2015, through September 1, 2015.
(Stipulation)
3. During the back pay period, Richardson's hourly rate of pay was $18.93, his
daily rate of pay was $227.16, and his bi- weekly rate of pay was $1,594.44. (Stipulation)
4. The initial thirty day grace period is from May 14, 2015, to June 12, 2015.
During this period of time, Richardson would have worked fifteen days. He is entitled to
$3,407.40 ($227.16 x 15) for the initial grace period. (Stipulation)
5. For the period of time between August 24, 2015 (the beginning of the week
in which the Commission final order issued) and Richardson's reinstatement on
September 2, 2015 (second grace period) he would have worked four days. Richardson
is entitled to $908.64 ($227.16 x 4) for the second grace period. (Stipulation)
6. There are thirty -seven work days between June 13, 2015, and August 23,
2015. Richardson would have worked two days during the week of May 10 and on
August 30 and September 1. He would have worked three days during the weeks of
May 17, May 31, June 14, June 28, July 12, July 26, August 9, and August 23. He would
have worked four days during the weeks of May 24, June 7, June 21, July 5, July 19,
August 2, and August 16. (Stipulation)
7. Richardson did not receive a distribution from Florida Retirement System
upon his dismissal. (Stipulation)
2

BP-2015-012
(Relates to CS-2015-065)
8. Officers receive a $150.00 uniform allowance every six months.
Richardson is entitled to a prorated uniform allowance of $112.50 for the period from
January through May 13, 2015. (Stipulation)
9. Richardson is entitled to $400.00 for special course incentive pay he would
have earned during the back pay period. (Stipulation)
10. At ACI, there is a significant need for employees to work overtime because
of staffing issues and the need to meet minimum manning requirements. Thus, officers
can usually work as much overtime as they desire. The amount of overtime Richardson
worked varied and depended on how tired he was and what was happening in his life at
any given time. He usually attempted to work fifteen to twenty hours of overtime a
month, but in December 2014 Richardson worked eighty hours of overtime and between
April 24 and May 13, 2015, he worked 34.5 hours of overtime. In addition, he was
planning on working more overtime in the summer of 2015 to make extra money. Based
on Richardson's history of working overtime, it is reasonable to infer that he would have
worked an average twenty -four hours of overtime per month during the back pay period
at the overtime rate of one and one -half times the regular hourly rate.
11. After Richardson was dismissed, he attempted to receive unemployment
compensation, but his application was denied. Thus, Richardson did not receive
unemployment compensation during the back pay period. The unemployment office
gave him a work search record form which he used to keep track of his job search efforts.
(Employee Exhibit 12)
3

BP-2015-012
(Relates to CS-2015-065)
12. Richardson lives in Greenwood, Florida, which is a small community south
of Malone and near the Florida, Georgia, and Alabama borders. There are very few job
opportunities in Greenwood. After being dismissed, he had to travel to larger cities to find
work. Richardson does not have a college degree. He has some prior experience as a
truck driver and he has maintained his commercial driver's license.
13. On May 19, 2015, he went to Walmart in Donalsonville, Georgia, seeking
any available position. However, he was told by the store manager that Walmart was not
hiring or taking applications. On June 9, he returned to Walmart and was able to submit
an application.
14. On May 25, Richardson sought a truck driver position with Paper Transport
International (PTI) in Cedar Springs, Georgia, but he was told PTI was not taking
applications. On June 15, he returned to PTI and submitted an application. He
interviewed for a position on July 22 and met with the company on August 20, when he
learned he did not get the job because he did not have sufficient experience.
15. On June 2, Richardson went to Jackson County Transportation, Inc.
(JTrans) in Marianna, but it was not hiring. He returned on June 23 and submitted an
application for a driver position. He followed up with JTrans in person on July 15, and he
was told they would get back to him.
16. On June 30, he submitted an application at Walmart in Marianna. On
July 29, he returned to Walmart seeking a clerk position. He was told that they would get
back with him.
4

BP-2015-012
(Relates to CS-2015-065)
17. On July 6, Richardson went to the Jackson County School Board, but it did
not have any jobs available at that time. He was told they would get back to him. On
August 12, he submitted an application for a skilled maintenance position.
18. On August 6, Richardson submitted an application with Waste Management
in Campbellton for a driver position. On August 25, he returned to Waste Management
and followed up on his application. He was told at that time that the company would get
back to him.
19. Richardson noted on the job search record how many miles he traveled
going to and from his home and the locations where he sought work. He traveled
618 miles conducting his job search.2 (Employee Exhibit 12)
20. Richardson paid his attorney, Matthew O. Ward, $2,000 for legal services
for the career service appeal. Between May and September 2015, Richardson drove
897 miles to file his appeal and meet with Ward about his case.
21. Richardson received health insurance through his job with the Agency. He
and the Agency each paid a portion of the premium. There is no evidence Richardson
obtained and paid for health insurance after he was dismissed. When he was reinstated,
Richardson had to pay $162.27 for his health insurance, which is a cost he would have
paid even if he had not been dismissed. (Employee Exhibit 8)
2Although Richardson notated on Employee Exhibit 12 that the total miles traveled
was 1,118, I have calculated the total as 618.
5

BP-2015-012
(Relates to CS-2015-065)
22. Richardson also had dental insurance through his Agency employment. In
September 2015, he had to pay $155.18 to bring the dental insurance current.
Richardson would have paid this amount for his dental insurance even if he had not been
dismissed. (Employee Exhibit 9)
23. Richardson has four loans with Focus Credit Union. After he was
dismissed, Richardson spoke with the branch manager because he could not afford to
make the monthly payments. The manager agreed to defer several monthly payments
until the end of the loans, thus causing Richardson to accrue more interest on the loans.
However, Richardson did not provide any evidence of how much additional interest he
will be required to pay.
24. On September 1, 2015, Richardson's daughter paid a car repair bill for him
in the amount of $343.39 because he could not afford to pay it. Richardson also
borrowed money from his parents to pay three utility bills. The April 15 to May 15, 2015,
bill was $154.51, the May 15 to June 15, 2015, bill was $210.02, and the July 15 to
August 15, 2015, bill was $310.04. Richardson intends to repay his daughter and
parents.
ISSUES
1. The amount of back pay to which Richardson is entitled.
2. Whether Richardson properly mitigated his damages.
6

BP-2015-012
(Relates to CS-2015-065)
ANALYSIS
In back pay proceedings, the Commission is required to approximate the earnings
an employee would have received absent his improper discharge. See Florida State
Lodge, Fraternal Order of Police v. Town of Pembroke Park, 10 FPER 1115001 (1983),
affd as clarified on denial of reh'q, 501 So. 2d 1294 (Fla. 4th DCA 1987). Here, the
parties agree that the back pay period ran from May 14, 2015, through September 1,
2015, and that Richardson would have earned $3,407.40 during the initial grace period
and $908.64 during the second grace period. The parties also agree that Richardson is
entitled to $112.50 for a prorated uniform allowance and $400.00 for special course
incentive pay.
The parties disagree whether Richardson should receive back pay for the period
between the two grace periods, that is between June 13, 2015, and August 23, 2015.
The parties also disagree about overtime compensation and reimbursement for various
expenses.
An employee who has been dismissed is responsible for attempting to mitigate his
damages. See DeMarois v. Military Park Fire Control Tax District No. 4, 9 FPER ¶ 14074
(1983), affd, 446 So. 2d 120 (Fla. 4th DCA 1984). The burden is on the employee to
prove his efforts. Lucas v. Department of Health and Rehabilitative Services, 11 FCSR
% 063 (1996). However, reasonable doubts as to the employee's mitigating efforts are
resolved in his favor because it was the employer's wrongful conduct which initially
7

BP-2015-012
(Relates to CS-2015-065)
caused the loss of employment. Florida State Lodge, Fraternal Order of Police v. Town
of Pembroke Park, 10 FPER ¶ 15001 (1983), affd as clarified on denial of reh'q,
501 So. 2d 1294 (Fla. 4th DCA 1987). Back pay will not accrue during any period of time
in which the employee is unavailable for work, out of the labor market, or fails to
demonstrate an active good faith job search. See Adams v. Department of Revenue,
14 FCSR 711 (1999), affd, 771 So. 2d 527 (Fla. 1st DCA 2000).
In Vickery v. Department of Corrections, 30 FCSR 79 (2015), the Commission
clarified the law on what constitutes a good faith effort to mitigate a job loss. The
Commission determined that it was not necessary for an employee to look for
comparable work in order to satisfy his obligation to conduct a good faith job search.
Rather, any job search done by an employee should be taken into consideration in
determining whether a good faith effort was made.
Here, as buttressed by his documentation, I have credited Richardson's testimony
that he looked for some type of work every week during the back pay period. Richardson
lives in a small community with few job opportunities so he personally visited employers
up to thirty miles from his home in the Jackson County area and in nearby cities in
Georgia. Based on his prior experience as a trucker and his having a commercial driver's
license, Richardson sought work at several trucking and transportation type companies.
He also applied several times for any available positions at two Walmarts and skilled
maintenance positions at the Jackson County School Board. At all these employers, he
filled out applications if they were being accepted, and he interviewed for one job. Thus,
8

BP-2015-012
(Relates to CS-2015-065)
Richardson made a good faith job search. Therefore, for the period between June 13,
2015, and August 23, 2015, Richardson is entitled to back pay in the amount of
$8,404.92 (37 work days x $227.16).
The Commission will compensate an employee for reasonable out -of- pocket
expenses incurred as a direct result of the loss of employment and fulfillment of the duty
to mitigate his damages. Barker v. Department of Environmental Protection, 10 FCSR
If 299 (1995). Richardson seeks to be reimbursed for the mileage he expended seeking
employment during the back pay period. According to his log, Richardson drove
618 miles. Traveling to various employers seeking employment is a reasonable and
necessary cost incurred as a result of his dismissal and duty to mitigate his damages.
See Lopez v. Department of Children and Families, 28 FCSR 142 (2013). However,
Richardson did not submit any evidence of the rate at which he should be reimbursed.
Thus, I apply the $0.445 per mile rate adopted in Section 112.061(7)(d)1 a, Florida
Statutes (2015), for state employees. Therefore, Richardson should receive $275.01 for
out -of- pocket mileage expenses.
Richardson requests that he be awarded overtime pay which he was not able to
earn during the back pay period because of his unlawful dismissal. The evidence reveals
that Richardson worked overtime on a consistent basis prior to being dismissed and that
he would have had the same opportunity to work overtime during the back pay period.
Based on the reasoning set forth in my facts, Richardson would have averaged twenty-
four hours per month of overtime during the back pay period. Since the back pay period
9

BP-2015-012
(Relates to CS-2015-065)
was approximately three and one -half months, Richardson is entitled to eighty -four hours
of overtime paid at the rate of $28.40, which is $2,385.60 in overtime pay. See Shiver v.
Department of Corrections, 30 FCSR 85 (2015).
There is no statutory or rule authority to award Richardson his attorney's fees for
either the merits of the career service appeal or the back pay case. Thus, his request to
be reimbursed for his attorney's fees is denied, as well as the miles he drove to file his
appeal and meet with his attorney.
Richardson is also not entitled to reimbursement for his utility bills or car repair bill.
He would have incurred these expenses even if he had not been dismissed. The fact
that he may owe other people for paying these bills for him does not make them a
reimbursable expense, particularly since there is no evidence he incurred any interest
expense. He can use the money he receives as back pay to pay off his debts to family
and friends.
Richardson also contends that he has additional interest to pay on some loans
because his credit union deferred several monthly payments until the end of the loan.
However, since Richardson did not provide a specific amount of additional interest he will
be required to pay, this request is denied.
Finally, Richardson requests that he be compensated for health and dental
insurance payments. Richardson did not present any evidence that he purchased
insurance to replace the insurance he lost when he was dismissed. In addition, it
10

BP-2015-012
(Relates to CS-2015-065)
appears that the money he expended for health and dental insurance after he was
reinstated were amounts he would have paid even if he had not been dismissed. Thus,
he is not entitled to any reimbursement for health or dental insurance costs.
CONCLUSIONS OF LAW
1. Richardson made a good faith job search during the back pay period.
2. Richardson is entitled to back pay in the amount of $15,894.07 ($8,404.92
in regular wages + $3,407.40 for the initial grace period + $908.64 for the second grace
period + $2,385.60 in overtime pay + $275.01 for mileage reimbursement + $400.00 in
incentive pay + $112.50 for uniform allowance), less lawful deductions, plus interest at
the lawful rate.
RECOMMENDATION
I recommend that the Commission ADOPT the foregoing recommended order and
award Richardson back pay as set forth above.
Any party may file exceptions to my recommended order, but exceptions must be
received by the Commission within fifteen days after the recommended order is issued.
See § 110.227(6), Fla. Stat. (2015); Fla. Admin. Code Rule 28- 106.104 and
28- 106.217(1). The Commission may not change the findings of fact or mitigation
recommendation (if any) in this order without first reviewing an official transcript of the
11

BP-2015-012
(Relates to CS-2015-065)
hearing. Any party who desires the Commission to review the transcript must file one
along with the exceptions.
ISSUED and SUBMITTED to the Public Employees Relations Commission in
accordance with Florida Administrative Code Rule 28- 106.216 and SERVED on all
parties this f day of October, 2015.
JOIN G. SHOWALTER
Hearing Officer

SHOWALTER, Hearing Officer.
The Department of Corrections (Agency) dismissed Renil G. Wickliffe from
employment. On August 31, 2015, the Commission issued an order mitigating Wickliffe's
dismissal to a thirty work -day suspension and awarding Wickliffe back pay. A back pay
case was established and a hearing was scheduled.
On October 12, 2015, a telephone hearing was conducted between Tallahassee
and Jacksonville.' All parties were provided with an opportunity to appear, present
evidence, examine witnesses, and fully participate in the hearing. Neither party filed a
written post- hearing document. A transcript of the hearing was not filed.
'Although the hearing was scheduled to be held between Tallahassee and Lake
City, Wickliffe and his attorney participated from the attorney's office in Jacksonville, thus
making it unnecessary to contact anyone at the institution in Lake City.

BP-2015-013
(Relates to CS-2015-072)
STIPULATIONS
1. At the time of Wickliffe's dismissal, he was a correctional officer working at
Columbia Correctional Institution (CCI). He worked the 7:00 a.m. to 7:00 p.m. shift.
2. Wickliffe was dismissed on May 13, 2015. The thirty work -day suspension
ran from May 14 through July 13. Wickliffe was reinstated on October 1. Thus, the back
pay period is from July 14 through September 30.
3. Wickliffe is not entitled to any back pay during the initial thirty day grace
period because he was still serving his suspension during that time.
4. Wickliffe's hourly rate of pay is $17.34 and his daily rate of pay is $208.08.
5. There were thirty -nine work days in the back pay period. There were
sixteen work days between August 31 and September 30.
6. Prior to deducting any interim earnings, Wickliffe is entitled to $8,115.12 in
back pay (39 work days x $208.08).
7. Wickliffe became employed by Tire Kingdom on July 13, 2015, which is
prior to the commencement of the back pay period. From July 11 through July 24 he
earned $873.90, from July 25 through August 7 he earned $825.04, from August 8
through August 21 he earned $476.28, from August 22 through September 4 he earned
$982.04 ($701.50 for the ten days in August and $280.60 for the four days in
2

BP-2015-013
(Relates to CS-2015-072)
September),2 from September 5 through September 18 he earned $901.25, and from
September 19 through October 2 he earned $628.09.
8. The total amount Wickliffe earned at Tire Kingdom was $4,686.60. He
earned $2,876.72 between July 13 and August 31.
9. Wickliffe is entitled to $3,428.52 in back pay if all of his Tire Kingdom
earnings are deducted from the pay he would have earned during the back pay period.
10. Wickliffe is entitled to $5,238.40 in back pay if his Tire Kingdom earnings
through August 31 are deducted from the pay he would have earned during the back pay
period.
11. Because Wickliffe obtained employment prior to the conclusion of the thirty
work -day suspension, he did not have any obligation to seek other employment or
otherwise mitigate his damages during the back pay period.
12. Any leave that Wickliffe was not paid for when he was dismissed will be
reinstated by the Agency.
13. The Agency will reinstate any fringe benefits, including insurance and
seniority, if it has not already done so.
14. Wickliffe did not receive a distribution from Florida Retirement System upon
his dismissal.
2Because of rounding in the calculation of these figures, there is a six cent
discrepancy.
3

BP-2015-013
(Relates to CS-2015-072)
ISSUE
The amount of back pay to which Wickliffe is entitled.
ANALYSIS
In back pay proceedings, the Commission is required to approximate the earnings
an employee would have received absent his improper discharge. See Florida State
Lodge, Fraternal Order of Police v. Town of Pembroke Park, 10 FPER 1115001 (1983),
affd as clarified on denial of reh'q, 501 So. 2d 1294 (Fla. 4th DCA 1987). Here, the
parties stipulated to all the necessary facts and amounts regarding back pay. There is
only one legal issue to be resolved, which is addressed later in this order.
The parties agree that Wickliffe was dismissed on May 13 and that the thirty work-
day suspension ran until July 13. The parties also agree that Wickliffe is not entitled to
any back pay during the first grace period because he was still serving his suspension.
Once the suspension ended on July 13, the back pay period began on July 14 and ran
until September 30. Since Wickliffe obtained employment before the back pay period
began, he did not have a further duty to mitigate his damages by continuing to seek work.
Vickery v. Department of Corrections, 30 FCSR 79 (2015) and Harrell v. Department of
Corrections, 30 FCSR 75 (2015). Thus, there is no issue in this case as to Wickliffe's job
search efforts.
4

BP-2015-013
(Relates to CS-2015-072)
Prior to any setoff for his earnings at Tire Kingdom, Wickliffe is entitled to
$8,115.12 for the back pay period. The parties have agreed that his total earnings at Tire
Kingdom were $4,686.60 and that his earnings between July 13 and August 31 were
$2,876.72.
The only dispute in this case is whether all of Wickliffe's earnings at Tire Kingdom
must be deducted from the back pay award or only the money he earned prior to the
issuance of the Commission's August 31 reinstatement order. Wickliffe argues that the
September earnings should not be deducted because he had no duty to mitigate his
damages after the date of the Commission order reinstating him. The Agency argues
that all his earnings should be deducted from his back pay award.
I agree with the Agency that all of Wickliffe's earnings at Tire Kingdom must be
deducted from his back pay award. The purpose of a back pay award is to make the
employee whole and place him in the position he would have been in had he not been
dismissed. See Florida State Lodge, Fraternal Order of Police v. Town of Pembroke
Park, 10 FPER % 15001 (1983), aff d as clarified on denial of reh'g, 501 So. 2d 1294 (Fla.
4th DCA 1987). If Wickliffe's September earnings are not deducted from his award, he
will receive a windfall and be in a better position than he otherwise would have been. In
addition, in Harrell v. Department of Corrections, 30 FCSR 75 (2015), the Commission
affirmed a hearing officer's determination that money earned after the issuance of the
reinstatement order had to be deducted from the back pay award.
5

BP-2015-013
(Relates to CS-2015-072)
Based on the foregoing, Wickliffe's award of $8,115.12 must be reduced by the
entire amount of his earnings at Tire Kingdom, $4,686.60. Therefore, Wickliffe is entitled
to a back pay award of $3,428.52, less lawful deductions, plus interest at the lawful rate.
RECOMMENDATION
I recommend that the Commission ADOPT the foregoing recommended order and
award Wickliffe back pay as set forth above.
Any party may file exceptions to my recommended order, but exceptions must be
received by the Commission within fifteen days after the recommended order is issued.
Sees 110.227(6), Fla. Stat. (2015); Fla. Admin. Code Rule 28- 106.104 and
28- 106.217(1). The Commission may not change the findings of fact or mitigation
recommendation (if any) in this order without first reviewing an official transcript of the
hearing. Any party who desires the Commission to review the transcript must file one
along with the exceptions.

DEPARTMENT OF CORRECTIONS, RECOMMENDED ORDER -
:
CORRECTIONAL OFFICER
Agency.
Matthew O. Ward, Tallahassee, attorney for employee.
Pamela L. Hatcher, Tallahassee, attorney for agency.
SALMON, Hearing Officer.
The Department of Corrections (Agency) dismissed Mark T. Raab for allegedly
violating several Agency and Department of Management Services rules, and he
appealed to the Commission. On September 16, 2015, after a procedural history
unnecessary to repeat here, the Commission issued an order reducing the disciplinary
penalty to a ten calendar day suspension and directing the Agency to reinstate Raab and
provide him with back pay and benefits, less any compensation and earnings which he
would not have received had his employment with the Agency not been interrupted. On
November 6, Raab filed an amended request for back pay and benefits.
Ori November 10, after due notice, an evidentiary hearing was conducted in
Tallahassee. All parties were afforded the opportunity to call witnesses, cross -examine
witnesses, and fully participate. The rule of sequestration was not invoked. At the close
of the hearing, Raab presented an oral closing argument. Thereafter, the Agency filed a
post- hearing document. Raab's oral closing argument and the Agency's post- hearing

BP-2015-015
(Relates to CS-2015-068)
document have been considered in preparing this recommended order. A transcript of
the hearing was not filed.
During the hearing, the parties entered into numerous factual stipulations. The
dispute between the parties involves Raab obtaining part-time employment. The issues
are whether an employee who obtains part-time employment has an obligation to
continue conducting a good faith job search and, if so, whether Raab conducted a good
faith job search after obtaining part-time employment.
FINDINGS OF FACT
Based on the record as a whole, I make the following findings:
Background - The Back Pay Period: May 21 to November 5, 2015
1. Prior to his dismissal, Raab worked as a correctional sergeant at Okaloosa
Correctional Institution. He worked twelve hour shifts, resulting in a total of eighty -four
hours in a biweekly pay period. (Stipulation)
2. On May 20, 2015, the Agency dismissed Raab. After a procedural history
unnecessary to repeat here, the Commission issued an order reducing the disciplinary
penalty to a ten calendar day suspension and directing the Agency to reinstate Raab and
provide him with back pay and benefits, less interim earnings.
3. The back pay period begins on May 21, the first day following his dismissal,
and ends on November 5, the day before the Agency reinstated Raab.
2

BP-2015-015
(Relates to CS-2015-068)
The First Grace Period: May 21 to June 19
4. There is a thirty day grace period (first grace period) immediately following
the dismissal in which Raab did not have to seek employment. The first grace period
began on May 21 and ended on June 19.
5. The ten calendar day suspension was served during the first grace period,
(May 21 to May 30). During these ten calendar days, Raab would have worked five
days. He is not entitled to back pay for this time period. (Stipulation)
6. For the remaining part of the first grace period, (May 31 to June 19), Raab
would have worked ten days. Raab's gross daily earning with the Agency was $205.20,
which includes $0.50 per hour for hazardous duty pay. He is entitled to $2,052.00 in
back pay. (Stipulation)
Whether Raab Conducted a Good Faith Job Search
7. After Raab learned that he would be dismissed by the Agency, he began
looking for employment. His goal was to find a career in which he could take care of his
family. To this end, he started looking for employment and kept looking in an effort to
find a "better" job.
8. Raab has a high school diploma. He retired from the Navy after achieving
the rank of Senior Chief (E -8), a management position where he trained mid -level
supervisors. His field of expertise was avionics and he is certified by the federal
communications commission. He is also certified as a correctional officer and has
3

BP-2015-015
(Relates to CS-2015-068)
certificates as a defensive tactics instructor, firearms instructor, and as a fitness
instructor.
9. Raab enjoys working with his hands, and he enjoys helping other people
who work with their hands. On June 16, prior to the end of the first grace period, Raab
began part-time employment with Home Depot. Raab's gross hourly rate at Home Depot
was $9.00. (Employee Ex. 1)
10. Beginning June 20, Raab was required to conduct a good faith job search.
Each week while employed at Home Depot, Raab would ask his supervisor to work more
hours and he would ask the assistant manager about being placed on full -time status. In
addition, on unspecified dates while working at Home Depot, he applied for positions with
L3 Communications (aeronautical maintenance), UTC Aerospace, International Paper
Company, AT &T (electrician), and Singapore Aerospace. He also applied to Pensacola
State College (teaching airborne electronics) and Locklin Tech. He received several
interviews and return interviews. He kept a "search log" but did not introduce it into
evidence.
11. From August 11 to August 31, Raab was unavailable for work. He is not
entitled to back pay for this time period. (Stipulation)
12. Had Raab worked each day at the Agency during the period he was
required to conduct a good faith job search, less the time he was unavailable to work, he
would have earned $6,156.00.1 (Stipulation)
'The $6,156.00 includes $457.80 for August 4 through August 10. (Stipulation)
4

BP-2015-015
(Relates to CS-2015-068)
The Second Grace Period: September 16 to November 5
13. On September 16, the Commission issued its order mitigating the dismissal
to a ten calendar day suspension. This begins the second grace period in which Raab
was no longer required to conduct a good faith job search. The second grace period
ended on November 5, the day before the Agency reinstated Raab. Raab is entitled to
$5,335.20. (Stipulation)
14. Raab's employment with Home Depot ended on November 6. His total
earnings from Home Depot were $3,199.50. (Stipulation; Employee Ex. 1)
15. Raab is entitled to $10,343.70 in gross back pay ($2,052.00 plus $6,156.00
plus $5,335.20 less $3,199.50 interim earnings)
16. Raab is not seeking reimbursement for uniform allowance or health, dental,
or vision insurance.
17. Raab did not apply for or receive unemployment compensation. He did not
want to remain unemployed long enough to receive it.
ANALYSIS
The back pay period is from May 21 to November 5, 2015. The back pay period
can be divided into three distinct periods of time: the first grace period; the period when
an employee is required to conduct a good faith job search; and the second grace
period. The parties amicably resolved Raab's entitlement to all back pay issues for the
5

BP-2015-015
(Relates to CS-2015-068)
first and second grace periods, which are the two ends of the back pay period
continuum. In between the two grace periods is that time when an employee is required
to conduct a good faith job search.
The first dispute between the parties involves Raab's obligation to conduct a good
faith job search after obtaining part-time employment with Home Depot. Raab argues
that obtaining part-time employment with Home Depot ended his obligation to conduct a
good faith job search. This contention may be supported by Vickery v. Department of
Corrections, 30 FCSR 79 at 81, Case No. BP- 2014 -015 (2015), wherein the Commission
stated that obtaining other employment ends the employee's duty to mitigate and,
therefore, the employee is entitled to back pay, without any requirement to continue
seeking a higher -paying job. The Agency contends that Raab enjoyed working at Home
Depot and saw it as an opportunity to move up in a different career. The Agency argues
that it is unlikely that the Commission's decision in Vickery was intended as a benefit to
employees which would allow them to transition into a more desirable career than to
search for comparable work at comparable wages.
This case presents the Commission with its first opportunity since Vickery to
determine the impact of an employee obtaining part-time employment on that employee's
obligation to continue a good faith job search. The resolution of the parties' dispute
requires a split recommendation. I agree with Raab, in part, and recommend to the
Commission that accepting part-time employment, which is what Raab did here, provides
6

BP-2015-015
(Relates to CS-2015-068)
evidence of a good faith job search. Albeit for a different reason, I agree with the Agency
that accepting a part-time job does not extinguish an employee's obligation to continue
conducting a good faith job search: a part-time job is not comparable to a full -time job.
Thus, Raab had an obligation to continue a good faith job search after obtaining part-
time employment at Home Depot. However, the analysis does not end here. The
second dispute between the parties is whether Raab conducted a good faith job search
while employed with Home Depot.
Raab testified that he continued his job search while working at Home Depot. The
Agency argues that Raab's testimony should be discredited because he failed to produce
any documentation substantiating a job search.
The lack of documentation is a factor which weighs against Raab's testimony that
he continued searching for a job after beginning work at Home Depot. Nevertheless,
Raab's testimony is credited that he sought, on a weekly basis, to turn the part-time job
at Home Depot into a full -time job. He enjoyed the job. It is reasonable to find that Raab
would not be provided with any documentation based on informal conversations with his
supervisor or the assistant store manager about potential openings. An additional factor
in Raab's favor is found in a review of Raab's earnings statements (Employee ex. 1). His
earning statements, which constitutes documentation, support his testimony that the
longer he worked for Home Depot the more he sought to increase his work hours (except
for the period of time in August when he was unavailable for work). Thus, I find that
7

BP-2015-015
(Relates to CS-2015-068)
Raab was motivated, on a weekly basis, to find a better paying job at Home Depot. This
is sufficient to demonstrate that Raab continued to look for a better job after being hired
by Home Depot.
Next, the Agency contends that Raab's testimony should not be credited because
of his attempt to defraud the State. According to the Agency, in August Raab received
wages from Home Depot while receiving temporary total worker's compensation benefits
based on an injury he had received while working for the Agency.
The Agency's contention is serious. However, the record is devoid of facts that
Raab's unavailability to perform work in August were due to a worker's compensation
claim. Without such facts in the record, there is insufficient evidence to discredit Raab's
testimony. Counterbalancing the Agency's contention is Raab deducting all interim
earnings that he received from Home Depot from his gross back pay, including his
August earnings, which reduced the Agency's back pay liability.
In sum, after Raab learned that he would be dismissed by the Agency, he began
looking for employment. This explains why he obtained employment with Home Depot
so quickly. After becoming employed by Home Depot, he continued looking for
employment in an effort to find a "better" job so he could take care of his family. His
credible testimony that he inquired about promotional opportunities on a weekly basis is
sufficient to satisfy his continuing obligation to conduct a good faith job search. Thus, I
find that Raab conducted a good faith job search while employed part-time at Home
Depot.
8

BP-2015-015
(Relates to CS-2015-068)
CONCLUSION OF LAW
Raab is entitled to $10,343.70 in back pay, less appropriate taxes and deductions
in back pay, plus interest at the lawful rate.
RECOMMENDATION
I recommend that the Commission incorporate this recommended order as part of
its final order and sustain the petition for back pay.
Any party may file exceptions to my recommended order, but exceptions must be
received by the Commission within fifteen days after the recommended order is issued.
See § 110.227(6), Fla. Stat. (2015); Fla. Admin. Code Rule 28- 106.104 and 28-
106.217(1). The Commission may not change the findings of fact or mitigation
recommendation (if any) in this order without first reviewing an official transcript of the
hearing. Any party who desires the Commission to review the transcript must file one
along with the exceptions.

accordance with Florida Administrative Code Rule 28- 106.216 and SERVED on all
parties this 3 R p day of November, 2015.
